info.title: FixMate API
info.summary: The JSON API the four FixMate applications talk to.
info.description:
A JSON API and nothing else: no route in it returns a page.

There are four sign-in doors, one per account type, and each resolves credentials against its own store. A person may hold an account in several stores under one address, so which store a request reaches is decided by the URL and never by the address in the body.

Every route below `/api/v1/identity` and above it is described by three artifacts that must agree: this document, `contract.json` (the front ends' recorded expectation), and the back end's route table. `php artisan api-docs:check` and `php artisan api-client:check` each hold one link of that chain.

servers.description: The application's own origin. Every path in this document is absolute, including the /api prefix, so that it can be compared to the back end's route table without arithmetic on a base path.

post.summary: Sign in as an end user.
post.description:
Resolves the credentials against the `users` store only, so it can only ever succeed for an account that exists there.

An unknown address, a wrong password and an account that cannot be used all answer with the same 422 and the same message, because telling them apart would make this endpoint a way of asking which addresses hold accounts.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.description: A separate door from the customer one, backed by a separate store. The worker is returned under `worker`, not under `user`, so a worker application is never handed a key it would have to special-case.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.description: A separate door from the super administrator one, backed by a separate store. An account that can sign in here carries no account-management ability; that is the distinction between the two administrator doors, and it is enforced here rather than in the interface.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.summary: Sign in as a super administrator.
post.description: The only path in the platform that issues the wildcard ability. The account is returned under `super_admin`.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.summary: Ask for a customer password reset link.
post.description:
Answers the same way whether or not the address holds an account, because a reset endpoint that reported an unknown address would be a way of asking which addresses do. A screen rendering the acknowledgement is showing a conditional statement and must not present it as "we have emailed you".

The store the address is looked for in is not a field, and must never become one: it is decided by the endpoint this request arrived at, so a client cannot ask for a link against a store that is not its own.

The link is single use and it is checked before the password is, so a password refused under `errors.password` leaves the link usable. A link that is spent or has expired is refused under `errors.password_reset` — a different failure with a different fix, told apart here even though neither says whether an account exists.

Not throttled, unlike the link request: this endpoint cannot be flooded with mail.

post.summary: Ask for a worker password reset link.
post.description: The same neutral acknowledgement as the customer door, against the `workers` store. Throttled separately from sign-in, and separately from the other three stores' reset doors, so flooding one store does not lock the same address out of another.

A separate operation from the customer one rather than a shared one with a parameter: the store a reset changes is decided by the endpoint, and a front end that could name the store would be able to ask for a link against an account that is not its own.

post.summary: Ask for an administrator password reset link.
post.description: Against the `admins` store, whichever store the address also happens to hold accounts in.
The same two refusal fields as every other reset, against the `admins` store.

post.summary: Ask for a super administrator password reset link.
Redeem a super administrator reset link.
post.description: The same two refusal fields as every other reset, against the `super_admins` store.

get.summary: Ask who the customer application's token belongs to.
get.description:
One door per application rather than one shared route, so that "a worker's token does not open the customer application" is a fact about a real address. A token presented at the wrong door is refused with a 403 that names both account types, which is safe to say because the caller has already proved they hold a working token.

`account_type` is in the response so a front end can notice it holds the wrong token. Without it, a mismatched token renders an empty dashboard rather than an error.

Worth calling at start-up rather than trusting a token handed over from storage: a suspended account is refused here with a 403, because an access token outlives the decision that issued it.

200.description: The account the token belongs to, and the abilities on the token.

get.summary: Ask who the worker application's token belongs to.
get.description: The same response as every other door, refused for the same reasons. The account type comes back as `workers`.

200.description: The account the token belongs to, and the abilities on the token.

get.description:
A super administrator function. The token must belong to a super administrator and carry `accounts:read`; an administrator is refused with a 403 whether or not the identifier in the path exists.

That is deliberate. A 404 for a record you may not see would make this endpoint a way of discovering which administrator accounts exist, so a caller that receives a 404 can be sure it was allowed to ask. The identifier is a positive integer, so anything else is a 404 rather than a server error.

The identifier is not a bound model, and must not become one: model binding resolves before the authorisation middleware runs, so a bound model would answer 404 for an identifier that does not exist and 403 for one that does — the same oracle, reintroduced.

bearerAuth.description: A Sanctum personal access token, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Opaque and not a JWT: read the claims it was issued with, from the `abilities` a `me` response echoes back, rather than decoding anything.

Acknowledgement.description: One message, and nothing else. Both halves of a password reset answer this way.

ValidationFailure.description:
The request was refused.

On a sign-in door this is also the answer for an unknown address, a wrong password and an account that cannot be used — all three are refused identically, under `errors.credentials`, and nothing in the response tells them apart.

refusedCredentials.summary: Credentials that do not resolve, in a store where they cannot.

value.message: These credentials do not match our records.

credentials: These credentials do not match our records.

refusedLink.summary: A reset link that is spent or has expired.

password_reset: This password reset link is no longer valid. Request a new one.

refusedPassword.summary: A new password that does not meet the policy. The link is still usable.

password: The password field must be at least 12 characters.

Unauthenticated.description: No usable token was presented. Carries a message and nothing else — in particular no stack trace, which a debug-mode exception would otherwise have appended to every refusal on this API.

Forbidden.description:
The token is valid and the caller still may not do this.

Three different situations answer here, and the message is what tells them apart: a token for another account type (which names both types, because the caller has proved they hold a working token), a token without the ability the route requires (which does not name the missing ability, because an oracle that hands out the access model one refusal at a time is the same mistake as confirming which addresses exist in a credential store), and a suspended account (which is not a signed-out state, so a front end must not send the person back to the sign-in screen).

NotFound.description: The record does not exist — answered only to a caller that was permitted to ask, so a 404 here is never a way of learning that a record exists and is merely hidden from you.

Throttled.description:
Too many attempts. Each door has its own allowance, so exhausting one does not lock the same address out of the other three.

`retry_after` is in seconds and matches the `Retry-After` header. This is the only refusal on the API that carries a second field: it is the one case where telling the caller when to come back is the useful answer.

Retry-After.description: Seconds to wait, matching `retry_after` in the body.

SignInAccount.description: An account as the sign-in doors return it: no status, because an account that cannot be used never gets here. There is no field for a password hash, and one could not be added without a field appearing here first.

ForgotPasswordRequest.description: An address and nothing else. The account type is not a field and must never become one.

token.description: The token from the reset link. Single use, and checked before the password, so a password refused under `errors.password` leaves the link usable.

password.description: The new password. Refused under `errors.password` when it does not meet the back end's policy.

Abilities.description: The token's own claim list, echoed back. Read it to decide what to offer before calling anything — but the back end re-checks it on every request, so hiding a button is a convenience and not the protection. `*` is the wildcard carried by a super administrator's token; `accounts:read`, `accounts:suspend` and `accounts:promote` are the named ones.

CurrentAccountResponse.description: The signed-in account, as the application that asked sees it. One shape for all four doors, unlike the sign-in responses above which nest the account under a per-type key. At sign-in each application already knows what it is; "who am I" is asked by a caller that may be holding the wrong token, so the answer has to be able to say that the thing answering is a customer when a worker was expected.

account_type.description: Which store the account is in. Read this before anything else: it is what tells a front end it is holding somebody else's token.

AdminAccountResponse.description: One administrator, as the account-management surface describes it. The same four fields as the account summary, deliberately, but a separate schema: this one is what a super administrator sees when looking at *someone else*, and each account type is meant to see a different representation of the same person. Sharing one schema would make that a matter of who remembered to unset a field.

ErrorResponse.description:
The shape of every refusal on this API. There is no envelope around it and no error code, deliberately: one shape for a validation failure, an unauthenticated request, a refused request and a missing record means a client has exactly one thing to read, and a second shape would be a second thing to get right.

`additionalProperties` is false because it is load-bearing. A debug-mode exception would otherwise append the file, the line and a stack trace to one of these, and the check that the key set is exactly `message` plus `errors` is what keeps it out.

errors.description: Per-field messages, present on a 422 and absent otherwise. The keys are `credentials` on a sign-in refusal, `password_reset` for a spent or expired link, and the field's own name otherwise — the same keys the back end's feature tests assert.

ThrottledResponse.description: The only refusal on the API that carries a second field, because this is the one case where when to come back is the useful answer.
